tasks.title: Write a script that runs an AWS CLI command and prints the result.
Configure a named profile and make your script use it explicitly rather than the default.
Add a check at the top that confirms your credentials work before doing anything else.
Install jq and pipe an AWS CLI response into it to see it formatted.
Extract one field from a JSON response with jq.
Use raw output so the value comes out without quotes and can be used in a variable.
Extract an array from a response and loop over its items in bash.
Use jq select to keep only the items matching a condition.
Use jq to build a smaller object containing only the fields you care about.
Use the AWS CLI query flag to return one field without using jq at all.
Use a query expression to filter a list by a property value.
Write down when you would use the query flag and when jq is the better choice.
Write a script that lists every IAM user in the account.
Extend it to show how old each access key is.
Flag any key older than ninety days and exit non zero if any are found.
Write a script that lists your VPCs with their CIDR blocks.
Extend it to list each subnet with its availability zone and CIDR.
Work out from the route tables which subnets are public and print that in the report.
Write a script that lists every security group and its inbound rules.
Find any rule that allows traffic from the whole internet.
Print a clear warning for each open rule, naming the group and the port.
Write a script that finds every NAT gateway in your account.
Loop the check across several regions so nothing is forgotten in one you never open.
Print a rough monthly cost estimate based on the hourly rate you recorded on day 58.
Write a script that lists running instances with their id, type and name tag.
Add filtering so it shows only instances with a tag you pass as an argument.
Format the output as aligned columns a human can read at a glance.

days.title: Launching And Tagging From A Script

tasks.title: Write a script that launches an instance from a launch template or AMI you pass in.
Tag it automatically with project, owner and a creation timestamp.
Wait until the instance reports running before the script exits.
Write a script that finds EBS volumes not attached to anything.
Extend it to find snapshots older than a number of days you choose.
Add a delete option that is off by default and prints what it would remove first.
Find every Elastic IP that is allocated but not attached to anything.
Find custom AMIs you created and their associated snapshots.
Combine both checks into one report of things quietly costing money.
Write a script that lists your buckets with their creation dates.
Extend it to report the size and object count of a bucket you name.
Write a sync script that uploads a folder and prints how many files changed.
Write a script that checks the public access block setting on every bucket.
Extend it to flag any bucket policy that allows access to everyone.
Add a check for default encryption and report any bucket without it.
Write a script that syncs a local folder to your website bucket.
Make it remove files from the bucket that no longer exist locally, with a confirmation.
Print the site URL at the end so you can click straight through to check it.
Write a script that lists RDS instances with their engine, class and status.
Flag any database that is publicly accessible.
Report the backup retention period for each and warn if it is zero.
Write a script that takes a snapshot of a volume or database you name.
Tag each snapshot with the date and the reason it was taken.
Delete snapshots created by the script that are older than your retention setting.
Write a script that lists your load balancers with their DNS names.
Report the health of every target in each target group.
Exit non zero and print a clear message if any target is unhealthy.
Write a script that lists every ACM certificate with its domain and status.
Calculate the days remaining until each one expires.
Warn on anything expiring within sixty days, reusing your day 41 logic.
Fetch CPU utilisation for one instance over the last hour from the CLI.
Parse the returned datapoints with jq and print the average.
Warn when the average is above a threshold you set.
Write a script that lists every CloudWatch alarm and its current state.
Show only the alarms currently in an alarm state.
Flag alarms stuck with insufficient data, since they are silently useless.
Write a script that reports your month to date spend.
Break the spend down by service and show the top five.
Compare this month against the same point last month and print the difference.
Create one script with a function per check, reusing the checks you built this month.
Group the security checks: IAM keys, open security groups, public buckets, public databases.
Give every check the same output format so the report reads as one document.
Add the cost section: orphaned volumes, unattached addresses, NAT gateways, old snapshots.
Print a summary at the top with the number of findings in each category.
Exit non zero when any high severity finding appears so it can run in a pipeline.
Turn your day 72 teardown checklist into a script that reports what is still running.
Make any destructive action require an explicit confirmation flag.
Run both tools against your account and fix everything they find.
Commit the audit and teardown tools to your repository with a README.

questions.prompt: Why name the profile explicitly in a script rather than relying on the default?
options: So the script cannot accidentally act on the wrong account
questions.explanation: Running a cleanup script against production because the default profile changed is a real failure mode.

questions.prompt: Why check your identity at the start of a script?
options: So you fail early with a clear message instead of midway through
questions.explanation: It is the same guard clause principle from day 8, applied to credentials.

questions.prompt: What format does the AWS CLI return by default?
questions.explanation: That is why jq and the query flag matter so much in AWS scripting.

questions.prompt: What does jq do?
questions.explanation: It is the standard tool for pulling values out of JSON on the command line.

questions.prompt: Why use raw output when extracting a value with jq?
options: So the value comes out without quotes and can be used directly
questions.explanation: A quoted string passed into another command usually breaks it.

questions.prompt: What does jq select do?
options: Keeps only the items matching a condition
questions.explanation: It is the filtering step, and it works like a where clause.

questions.prompt: What is the AWS CLI query flag for?
options: Selecting and filtering fields server side in the response
questions.explanation: It uses JMESPath and often removes the need for jq entirely.

questions.prompt: When is jq the better choice over the query flag?
options: When you need to reshape or combine data beyond simple selection
questions.explanation: The query flag handles selection well, and jq handles transformation.

questions.prompt: Why audit the age of IAM access keys?
options: Because old keys are more likely to have leaked and are often forgotten
questions.explanation: Key rotation is a basic control, and nobody does it manually.

questions.prompt: Why should an audit script exit non zero when it finds a problem?
options: So it can be used as a gate in a pipeline
questions.explanation: Exit codes are how automation acts on results, as you learned on day 7.

questions.prompt: Why loop a check across several regions?
options: Because forgotten resources in unused regions still cost money
questions.explanation: This is exactly the problem the day 51 advice about picking one region was warning about.

questions.prompt: What makes a report script genuinely useful?
options: A clear summary a human can act on
questions.explanation: A report nobody reads is the same as no report.

questions.prompt: The AWS CLI returning JSON is the main reason jq is worth learning early.
questions.explanation: Almost every AWS scripting task starts with pulling a value out of a JSON response.

questions.prompt: A script that acts on whichever profile happens to be default is safe enough for personal use.
questions.explanation: Defaults change, and the mistake it enables is destructive and easy to make.

questions.prompt: Auditing is mostly about comparing what exists against what should exist.
questions.explanation: That is the same idea behind firewall audits, drift detection and security reviews.

questions.prompt: How would a script determine whether a subnet is public?
options: Check whether its route table has a route to an internet gateway
questions.explanation: It is the route table that decides, exactly as you learned on day 56.

questions.prompt: What does a security group rule allowing the whole internet look like?
questions.explanation: That is the pattern an audit script should always flag for review.

questions.prompt: Is every rule open to the internet automatically wrong?
options: No, but each one should be deliberate and justified
questions.explanation: A public web server needs port 443 open, and an open SSH port usually does not belong.

questions.prompt: Why estimate NAT gateway cost in a script?
options: Because it bills hourly whether used or not and is easy to forget
questions.explanation: It is one of the most common causes of an unexpected AWS bill.

questions.prompt: Why tag resources automatically at creation time?
options: Because tags added later are usually never added at all
questions.explanation: Automatic tagging is the only tagging that stays consistent.

questions.prompt: What should a launch script wait for before exiting?
options: The instance to reach a running state
questions.explanation: Exiting immediately leaves the caller unsure whether the launch actually worked.

questions.prompt: Why format list output as aligned columns?
options: Because unreadable output means the tool goes unused
questions.explanation: Usability decides whether you actually run your own tools.

questions.prompt: Why filter instances by tag rather than listing everything?
options: Because a real account has too many resources to scan by eye
questions.explanation: Filtering is what makes a tool work at more than toy scale.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of a script that can delete resources?
options: One bad filter deletes the wrong things across the whole account
questions.explanation: The blast radius of a broken loop is every resource it matches.

questions.prompt: How should a delete option behave by default?
options: Print what it would delete without deleting anything
Ask for confirmation on each item
questions.explanation: A dry run by default means a mistake costs you nothing.

questions.prompt: Why do orphaned volumes and snapshots matter?
options: They keep billing even though nothing uses them
questions.explanation: Storage bills independently of instances, as you learned on day 65 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: What is the connection between this month and your Terraform work later?
options: Auditing what exists is the manual version of drift detection
questions.explanation: You are learning to compare intended state against actual state before you meet the tool that automates it.

questions.prompt: A destructive script should require an explicit flag before it deletes anything.
questions.explanation: Defaults should be safe, and destruction should always be a deliberate choice.

questions.prompt: Tagging resources at creation is more reliable than tagging them afterwards.
questions.explanation: Manual tagging afterwards is the step everyone skips when they are busy.

questions.prompt: An audit script only needs to run once, when the account is set up.
questions.explanation: Accounts drift constantly, which is why the audit is something you schedule.

questions.prompt: Why check the public access block setting on every bucket?
options: Because a publicly readable bucket is a common cause of data leaks
questions.explanation: It is the single most valuable S3 check you can automate.

questions.prompt: What in a bucket policy should an audit flag?
options: A policy granting access to everyone
A policy naming your own account
questions.explanation: A principal of everyone is what makes a bucket effectively public.

questions.prompt: Why check default encryption on buckets?
options: So new objects are encrypted without anyone remembering to do it
questions.explanation: A default means the safe option happens without depending on discipline.

questions.prompt: Why should a sync that deletes remote files ask for confirmation?
options: Because a wrong local path could wipe the entire bucket
questions.explanation: Delete on sync is powerful and unforgiving, which is exactly when confirmation matters.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of sync over copying everything each time?
questions.explanation: Reduced transfer means faster deploys and lower cost.

questions.prompt: Why print the site URL at the end of a deploy script?
options: So you can immediately verify the deploy worked
questions.explanation: Small conveniences are what make you keep using your own tools.

questions.prompt: Why flag a publicly accessible database?
options: Because it should almost never be reachable from the internet
questions.explanation: This is the same reasoning behind putting databases in private subnets on day 66.

questions.prompt: What does a backup retention period of zero mean?
questions.explanation: It means there is no automatic recovery point, which is worth a loud warning.

questions.prompt: Why tag snapshots with the reason they were taken?
options: So you can tell later which are safe to delete
questions.explanation: Untagged snapshots accumulate because nobody dares delete something they cannot identify.

questions.prompt: Why should a snapshot pruning script only delete snapshots it created?
options: Because deleting someone else's backup could destroy a recovery point
questions.explanation: Scoping destructive actions to your own resources is a basic safety rule.

questions.prompt: What should a bucket size report be used for?
options: Finding where storage cost is actually going
questions.explanation: You cannot reduce a cost you cannot locate.

questions.prompt: Why combine several small checks into one audit script?
options: So the whole picture appears in one run instead of several
questions.explanation: A single command that reports everything is a tool you will actually run.

questions.prompt: A default that makes the safe thing happen automatically is better than relying on people remembering.
questions.explanation: This principle applies to encryption, tagging, backups and dry runs alike.

questions.prompt: A sync with delete enabled and a wrong source path can empty a bucket.
questions.explanation: It is why the confirmation step exists, and why versioning matters even more.

questions.prompt: Checking backup retention is part of a security audit rather than a reliability audit.
questions.explanation: It belongs to reliability and recovery, though a good audit script covers both areas.

questions.prompt: What does the target health check on a load balancer tell you?
options: Whether each backend is receiving traffic
questions.explanation: An unhealthy target is removed from the pool, which is the failure most worth alerting on.

questions.prompt: Why check ACM certificates across the whole account?
options: Because one forgotten expiry can take down a service
questions.explanation: Certificates expire silently until the moment they cause an outage.

questions.prompt: Why warn sixty days before a certificate expires rather than seven?
options: Because renewal and validation can take time to arrange
questions.explanation: The warning has to arrive while there is still time to act calmly.

questions.prompt: What does fetching CloudWatch metrics from the CLI return?
options: A list of datapoints over a time range
questions.explanation: You then have to aggregate them yourself, which is what jq is for.

questions.prompt: Why calculate an average rather than reading a single datapoint?
options: Because one datapoint can be an outlier that means nothing
questions.explanation: Trends matter more than instantaneous values for almost every metric.

questions.prompt: What does an alarm in the insufficient data state mean?
options: It is not receiving the metric and is therefore not protecting anything
questions.explanation: A silently useless alarm is worse than no alarm, because you believe you are covered.

questions.prompt: Why list alarms currently in an alarm state?
options: So you see active problems without opening the console
questions.explanation: A single command that answers is anything broken right now is genuinely useful.

questions.prompt: Why break down cost by service?
options: Because the total tells you nothing about what to change
questions.explanation: You need to know which service to look at before you can reduce anything.

questions.prompt: Why compare this month against the same point last month?
options: Because a rising trend is more meaningful than an absolute number
questions.explanation: A jump against the same period is the signal that something changed.

questions.prompt: What should a metric warning threshold be based on?
questions.explanation: This is the same reasoning you will meet again when you set real alerts in Month 8.

questions.prompt: Why is a cost script part of an engineer's toolkit rather than finance's?
options: Because architectural choices drive the bill and engineers make those choices
questions.explanation: You own the decisions, so you own part of the outcome.

questions.prompt: What do these monitoring scripts prepare you for later?
options: The observability work in Month 8, where the same ideas are automated properly
questions.explanation: Golden signals, thresholds and alert noise all come back with better tooling.

questions.prompt: An alarm that never receives its metric is effectively no alarm at all.
questions.explanation: It gives false confidence, which is worse than knowing you have no coverage.

questions.prompt: Aggregating CloudWatch datapoints yourself is a reasonable way to learn what dashboards do for you.
questions.explanation: Doing it by hand once makes the managed version far easier to reason about.

questions.prompt: Cost is only worth checking at the end of the month.
questions.explanation: By then the money is spent, which is why day 54 made you check the dashboard daily.

questions.prompt: Why give every check in an audit tool the same output format?
options: So the whole report reads as one document rather than several
questions.explanation: Consistency is what turns a pile of scripts into a tool.

questions.prompt: Why put a summary of finding counts at the top of a report?
options: So the reader knows immediately whether anything needs attention
questions.explanation: Nobody reads a long report to discover there was nothing wrong.

questions.prompt: Why should an audit tool exit non zero on high severity findings?
options: So it can act as a gate in a pipeline
questions.explanation: That single behaviour is what lets a script become part of automation.

questions.prompt: What separates a security finding from a cost finding?
options: One is about exposure and the other about waste
questions.explanation: Both matter, and grouping them helps the reader act on the right things first.

questions.prompt: Why automate the teardown checklist?
options: Because a manual checklist gets skipped when you are tired
questions.explanation: The checklist exists precisely for the moments when you are least likely to follow it.

questions.prompt: How should a teardown tool behave by default?
options: Report what is still running without deleting
questions.explanation: Report first and destroy only on an explicit flag is the safe default.

questions.prompt: Why require a confirmation flag for destructive actions?
options: So destruction is always deliberate rather than accidental
questions.explanation: The flag is a small friction that prevents an expensive mistake.

questions.prompt: What does building an audit tool teach you beyond bash?
options: What good and bad configuration actually look like in a real account
questions.explanation: You cannot write a check without first understanding what it is checking for.

questions.prompt: Why commit these tools to your repository?
options: Because they are portfolio evidence that you understand cloud operations
questions.explanation: A working audit tool says more about you than a list of services on a CV.

questions.prompt: What should the README for these tools explain?
options: What each tool checks, how to run it, and what its exit codes mean
questions.explanation: Someone should be able to run it without reading the source.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest risk in an account audit tool?
options: A broken filter causing it to act on the wrong resources
It uses too many API calls
questions.explanation: Which is why dry run defaults and confirmation flags exist.

questions.prompt: What have these three months of bash actually built toward?
options: The ability to automate the operational work the main track taught you
questions.explanation: Bash is the glue, and from Month 4 Python takes over the heavier work.

questions.prompt: A tool that reports problems but cannot be run automatically is only half finished.
questions.explanation: The exit code and consistent output are what let it run unattended.

questions.prompt: An audit tool you wrote yourself is stronger interview material than a certificate alone.
questions.explanation: It demonstrates that you understand what good configuration looks like, not just that you studied it.

questions.prompt: From next month the daily track moves to Python, and bash stops being useful.
questions.explanation: Bash remains the glue for everything small, and Python takes over where bash becomes awkward.
